articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Entities, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC removed certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea, indicating a recalibration of sanctions policy in these areas.

In addition to the designations and removals, OFAC issued new general licenses pertaining to Iran and Russia. These licenses aim to authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, potentially easing humanitarian or other specific activities.

The Treasury Department also published amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) to provide further guidance on the updated sanctions programs and the scope of the new general licenses. This aims to help individuals and entities understand and comply with the revised regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes PAIPA Designations on Chinese Entities for Intellectual Property Theft
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. These designations target entities involved in the theft of American intellectual property.

China's Ministry of Commerce spokesperson stated that China firmly opposes the U.S. sanctions on five Chinese entities under the PAIPA, citing 'theft of trade secrets.' Beijing urged the U.S. to correct its actions and warned of necessary countermeasures to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued associated General Licenses to provide specific authorizations for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited. This aims to mitigate unintended consequences while maintaining the pressure on those engaged in intellectual property theft.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License on October 16, 2026. This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Venezuela.

Alongside the amended General License, OFAC also updated its Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to Venezuela sanctions. These updates provide additional clarity and guidance for individuals and entities navigating the complex Venezuelan sanctions regime.
The changes aim to refine the scope of permissible activities under the sanctions program, potentially in response to ongoing developments in Venezuela or policy adjustments by the U.S. government.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian and Cuban Entities, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026. These actions target entities and individuals deemed to be involved in activities contrary to U.S. foreign policy and national security interests.

Specifically, OFAC sanctioned Hong Kong-based Elitesphere Trading Co. Limited for its alleged ties to Iran, accusing it of being used by Farab Sorough Qeshm Company to move funds through a network of brokers and front companies to evade sanctions. This network reportedly moves funds through Hong Kong to the UAE and Türkiye, where they are converted to gold and cash and then smuggled to Iran and its proxies.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions. These updates are intended to provide clarity and guidance on the scope of the new sanctions and any authorized transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation on October 14, 2026. This action indicates a de-listing of an individual or entity previously subject to U.S. sanctions.

Designation removals typically occur when the sanctioned party meets certain criteria, such as demonstrating a change in behavior or providing evidence that the basis for the original designation no longer applies.
Such removals can signal a potential shift in U.S. policy or a recognition of efforts made by the de-listed party to comply with international norms and regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities on October 13, 2026. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to disrupt illicit financial networks supporting criminal and terrorist organizations.

These designations aim to isolate the targeted individuals and entities from the international financial system, preventing them from accessing resources that could be used to fund their illicit operations.
The Treasury Department regularly employs such measures to combat global threats, working to safeguard the U.S. financial system from abuse by those engaged in drug trafficking and terrorism.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026. This license authorizes certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under existing sanctions against Russia.

General Licenses are often issued to permit specific types of activities, such as humanitarian aid, certain financial transactions, or other operations deemed necessary or in the U.S. national interest, without requiring individual applications.
This new issuance reflects ongoing adjustments to the Russia sanctions program, potentially in response to evolving geopolitical circumstances or to address specific operational needs.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Entities, Amends Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026. These actions target individuals and entities involved in activities supporting the Iranian regime.

Concurrently, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License and an amended Russia-related General License. These licenses aim to provide specific authorizations for certain transactions, balancing sanctions pressure with other policy considerations.
The amended Russia-related General License indicates a continuous evaluation and adjustment of the sanctions framework in response to the dynamic situation involving Russia.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11,662,930 in Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to a settlement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for $11,662,930. This settlement resolves apparent violations of various sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The OFAC settlement is part of a broader enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury Department, which also included a $1.2 billion penalty from FinCEN and a $750 million civil money penalty from the OCC for deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act/anti-money laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program.

Bank of America admitted to willful violations of the BSA, including failures to implement and maintain an adequate AML program, conduct due diligence for foreign correspondent accounts, and file suspicious activity reports for over $5 billion in transactions.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has reached a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for $175,015. This settlement addresses apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

The details of the violations leading to this settlement were not immediately disclosed in the public announcement, but such agreements typically involve unauthorized transactions or dealings with sanctioned entities or jurisdictions.

OFAC enforcement actions aim to ensure compliance with U.S. sanctions programs and deter future violations by individuals and companies operating within U.S. jurisdiction or engaging in U.S.-nexus transactions.

articles.headline: Saudi Aramco Boosts Pipeline Capacity Amid Strait of Hormuz Tensions
body: Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil company, Aramco, has significantly increased the volume of oil moving through a pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz, tripling its capacity from 2 million to 7 million barrels per day. This move comes amidst heightened tensions in the Middle East, including attacks on Saudi oil facilities by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants.

The East-West pipeline, originally built in the early 1980s, has become crucial for Saudi Arabia's oil exports, especially during disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. President Trump recently accused Iran of fabricating attacks on ships in the Strait to drive up oil prices before the U.S. midterm elections.

The price of Brent crude oil surged by approximately 4% to $113 per barrel after Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed attacks on four vessels near the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. military has also reportedly reduced its footprint in the Middle East due to ongoing threats and attacks by Iran and its allies.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Significant Enforcement Actions Against American Express National Bank and Bank of America
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced enforcement actions for October 2026, including substantial penalties against American Express National Bank and Bank of America, National Association. American Express National Bank received a Cease and Desist Order and a $350 million civil money penalty for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and violations related to customer due diligence and identification programs.

Bank of America, National Association, was assessed a $750 million civil money penalty for similar deficiencies in its BSA compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. These actions underscore the OCC's commitment to holding banks accountable for maintaining effective BSA/AML compliance programs.

The OCC also issued Orders of Prohibition against two institution-affiliated parties: Jennifer Hamblin, a Vault Teller at Fifth Third Bank, N.A., for embezzling approximately $292,000 in customer funds, and Christopher Organista, a Former Operations Processor at U.S. Bank National Association, for embezzling approximately $194,131 in bank customer funds. These individual actions reinforce accountability for misconduct within financial institutions.

articles.headline: OCC Releases Report on Debanking Practices, Signals Further Regulatory Changes
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its long-awaited report, 'Guaranteeing Fair Banking for All Americans,' on October 14, 2026, detailing the debanking practices of the nine largest national banks it supervises. The report concludes that between 2020 and September 2025, these banks maintained policies or practices that may have led to the denial or limitation of financial services based on customers' political or religious beliefs or lawful business activities.

While the OCC did not announce any immediate enforcement actions or penalties, Comptroller Jonathan Gould expressed a lack of confidence in the banks' current remedial efforts and indicated that the OCC would be assessing further changes to the regulatory and supervisory framework. The OCC is also considering actions to prevent discrimination based on political or religious beliefs and to address the role of reputation risk in bank decision-making.

This report follows Executive Order 14331, 'Guaranteeing Fair Banking for All Americans,' issued in August 2025, which directed federal banking regulators to review institutions for politicized or unlawful debanking. In April 2026, federal banking agencies issued a final rule prohibiting regulators from using reputation risk in certain contexts.

body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. (bank), for violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and its implementing regulations, including 12 CFR 21.21 and 12 CFR 21.11. This amount is the largest in OCC history.

articles.headline: FinCEN Assesses $1.2 Billion Penalty Against Bank of America for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) announced a $1.2 billion civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. for its willful failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including those related to Chinese Money Laundering Networks and illicit finance along the southwest border.

Bank of America admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) by failing to implement and maintain an adequate anti-money laundering (AML) program, conduct due diligence for correspondent accounts for foreign financial institutions, and file Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs).

This penalty is part of a coordinated enforcement action, with FinCEN crediting $750 million of its assessment against a concurrent civil money penalty imposed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) for the bank's deficient BSA/AML compliance program. The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) also announced an $11.6 million settlement with the bank for sanctions violations.

Administrative enforcement settlements typically involve civil penalties, such as fines, and may include other conditions to ensure future compliance with U.S. export control laws.
BIS regularly pursues enforcement actions against companies that violate the EAR, which governs the export and reexport of most commercial items, including dual-use goods and technologies.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
